Posterity means all the people who will live after us in the future — every generation that comes after the current one. It refers to future human beings as a whole group, not any one specific person.

Think of it like a long river of time. You are standing somewhere in the middle of that river. Everyone who already lived is behind you (the past). Posterity is everyone who will exist ahead of you — your children, their children, their grandchildren, and every human being who will ever be born after this moment, stretching far into the future.

Posterity is a collective noun, meaning it refers to a group as a single unit — much like how "humanity" means all humans together, not just one person. You wouldn't say "a posterity" or "three posterities." You simply say posterity, and it means all future generations bundled together as one idea.

✅ "We must protect the forests for posterity."
❌ "We must protect the forests for a posterity."

1. Posterity = All Future Generations (General)

In this sense, posterity means the whole of humanity that is yet to come — not your personal family, but everyone who will ever live after us.

"These ancient cave paintings were preserved so that posterity could understand how early humans lived."

Here, "posterity" means people living thousands of years from now who will study these paintings.

"The decisions we make today about climate change will affect posterity for centuries."

2. Posterity = One's Own Descendants (Personal)

Sometimes, posterity is used more personally to mean your own future family line — your children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and so on.

"The king built a vast empire, hoping to leave a lasting legacy for his posterity."

Here it means his own bloodline and heirs, not all of humanity.

Both uses are correct. Context tells you which one is meant, but both carry the same basic idea: people who come after.

By far the most common way you will encounter this word is in the phrase "for posterity." This phrase means: doing or saving something so that future generations will have it, remember it, or benefit from it.

It carries the idea that something is worth preserving across time.

"The interview was recorded for posterity." (= so future people can watch it and remember this moment)

"She kept all of her grandfather's letters for posterity." (= so the family's future generations would have them)

"Let's take a photo for posterity!" (= so we have a record of this moment to look back on)

This phrase is also sometimes used with light humor in everyday speech — someone might say "let's save this embarrassing video for posterity" as a joke, playing on the grand, serious tone of the word.

Posterity is a formal and somewhat solemn word. It carries a sense of weight and importance. When someone uses it, they are usually trying to say that something matters beyond the present moment — that it has significance that will echo through time.

You'll most often find it in:

  • Historical writing and speeches
  • Philosophy and literature
  • Serious journalism
  • Legal and political documents

It is not a casual, everyday word. You wouldn't normally hear it in informal conversation. But understanding it helps you read serious texts more deeply.

This is worth being clear about, because the word can seem slippery:

  • It does not refer to the past. The opposite of posterity — people who lived before us — are called our ancestors, forebears, or predecessors.
  • It does not refer to the present. It strictly means future people.
  • It is not a synonym for "popularity" or "fame." Those are unrelated words. Posterity is purely about future generations of people, not about how well-known something is.

Here are a few more sentences to sharpen your feel for the word:

"Abraham Lincoln's speeches were written not just for his time, but for posterity."

"Will posterity judge us kindly for how we treated the planet?"

"The scientist published her findings so that posterity might build upon her work."

"He had no children and worried about what he would leave behind for posterity."

If you ever need to recall this word instantly, remember this:

Posterity = all the people who will live after us, especially as the audience or inheritors of what we do today.

It is the idea that our actions, creations, and choices outlive us — and that the people of the future are watching, even if they haven't been born yet.
